Some, but not by a lot, I don't think.

Science requires "peer review" - but that relies on what exactly a "peer" is. And most of the people who would be considered "peers" already have access to these papers one way or the other. They'd consider general members of the public expressing opinions on the papers to not be their peers.

It would possibly help call out what sort of studies are being run, and who they're funded by, but there are more than a few journalists on all sides of the arguments reviewing the publications and pointing out the ones they find suspicious.

One thing it would do is make taxpayer-funded science more available to everyone, which would tend to improve people's lives, so there's that, which is nice.

The likely implications would be two fold with one generally being a good thing and the other being a bad thing if kept unchecked.

The good part. Transparency would likely increase accountability in so far as what gets funded and outsider challenges to the legitimacy of studies. Allowing people greater access to academic studies could help the public contextualize scientific results. It's often the case that a limited study will come out with politically relevant results. Never mind that these results are not in line with all the other studies on the topic or there are just no studies corroborating these results. The media jumps to 11 and the public is stuck with yet another "scientific" truth that is of very little value. Even meta studies where scientists do a run down of how many studies support or oppose a theory (climate change has had issues here) fall into this same trap. I'm not big on meta studies because they are methodologically ill formed. 100 poorly performed experiments does not negate 1 really good experiment. If you don't have access to the underlining studies such reports are of minimal value. It is sometimes the case that a lot of the studies share similar methodological limitations. I'm not trying to be ascientific here merely pointing out the limitations of the public dialogue with the scientific community. Anyways greater access could lead to novel ideas about methodology and open up avenues for scientific discovery particularly in the social sciences where bias can have a very large effect. Instead of being force fed a scientific narrative the public could provide an important check on the biases inherent to academics.

The bad part. Sometimes more information is just not useful. On any given topic you can find papers supporting most positions wherein the difference is due to outright dishonesty, biased methodology, or exigent factors (e.g. it's possible that differing cultural attitudes across our country could lead to differing results in a sociological study performed in NYC vs rural Georgia or a study performed twenty years ago will not replicate with the same results under the same conditions in the current year). Depending on what you consider science there is a greater rate of replicability (the ability of independent people to verify the results) and the importance of the "average" study performed in a field (depending on the field studies the "average" study is cited at different rates). I'm hoping most of this isn't news to you but anyways. Opening up more of this to the public could lead scientists having to spend a lot of effort explaining already explained phenomenon to the public. While this isn't necessarily a bad thing it could lead to a greater confusion among the public about what is "true". You could have misguided and disingenuous people popping up to support bad science for political reasons which of course happens currently but possibly at a greater rate.
